the 'intelligible principle” test suggests that, beyond signaling a powerful 
resistance to judicial second guessing of legislatively specified standards for 
administrative action, the Court never seems to have given that “test” much 
serious thought concerning its operational consequences. And if that is true, it 
is hard not to concede that “intelhgible principle” is a pretty flabby criterion 
for determining whether statutory standards are sufficient to permit either 
legal or pofitical oversight of whether agencies have adhered to the criteria for 
judgment that Congress intended to guide administrative action. And that, 
Justice Gorsuch argues, is the critical separation of powers concern that fies 
behind the non-delegation doctrine.
The question is what might function as a more appropriate substitute. 
Justice Gorsuch’s analysis features references to cases where the Court seemed 
to focus on whether the administrator’s job was just to find “facts” or “fill in the 
details.” But what counts as a “fact” or a “detail”? If he really means just facts, 
imencumbered by any judgments of policy, then most delegations of authority 
to administrators are unconstitutional. When the National Labor Relations 
Board determines whether certain workers are “employees” under the 
National Labor Relations Act (see NLRB v. Hearst in Chapter 7) it is not 
finding a fact. Whether Hearst’s “newsboys” were employees or independent 
contractors for purposes of appfication of the NLRA is a conclusion of law and 
pohcy—or perhaps a mixed question of law and fact. To be sure, that conclusion 
must be based on findings of fact about the workers’ circumstances. But 
whether those facts mean that they are employees necessarily involves a poficy 
judgment about whether those circumstances warrant the appfication of the 
NLRA’s protections to those workers. And it would be hard know whether a 
similar NLRB finding today about Uber’s drivers was a mere “detail” in the 
appfication of the NLRA, or a major poficy judgment affecting a nationwide 
work force, and perhaps labor relations in the whole of the so-called “gig” 
economy. The latter position is arguably more persuasive. Does Justice 
Gorsuch mean to lay waste much of the U.S. Code related to administrative 
implementation with a rigorous “fact” or “detail” test? A serious “fact” or 
“detail” test would surely do so.
If Justice Gorsuch does not mean to do this, that leaves open the question 
of what a new test might be for determining whether statutory criteria for 
administrative judgment are sufficient to permit legal and pofitical oversight 
and, thus, administrative accountability to legal and pofitical overseers. For, 
as Justice Gorsuch tells us, that is the real separation of powers issue—^not 
whether the administrative judgment is properly characterized as a fact or a 
detail. Stay tuned.
